title: Senior's toolkit: undo and recovery
summary: reflog, reset, restore, revert and stash with the flags that get you out of trouble fast.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: undo and recovery
steps.body: Almost nothing in Git is lost once it was committed. These commands find it again and put it back, and each one has a safe and a dangerous form.

toolkit.what: Every position HEAD (or a branch) has been at, newest first. It is how you find commits that a reset, rebase or amend left behind.
flags: the history of one branch instead of HEAD
toolkit.when: a commit seems to have vanished

toolkit.what: Moves the branch back to where it was n moves ago, according to the reflog. The standard undo for a bad reset or rebase.
flags: where HEAD was one move ago
where HEAD was before the last reset, merge or rebase
like `--hard`, but refuses to overwrite uncommitted edits
toolkit.when: after `git reflog` shows the entry you want

toolkit.what: Undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged, ready to commit again. `--mixed` (the default) keeps them unstaged; `--hard` throws them away.
flags: move the branch and reset the index
toolkit.when: the commit is local and you want to redo it

toolkit.what: Brings one file back from any commit without touching anything else.
flags: where to take the content from (default: the index)
restore both the index and the file

toolkit.what: Adds a new commit that undoes an old one. The safe undo for anything already pushed to a shared branch.
flags: revert a merge commit, keeping parent 1 (the branch you merged into)
stage the revert without committing, to revert several at once
toolkit.when: a pushed commit or merge broke main

toolkit.what: Shelves your uncommitted work so you can switch tasks, with a name you will recognise later.
flags: include untracked files (new files are left behind without it)
a message shown in `git stash list`
stash, but leave staged changes in place

toolkit.what: Find a stash, read it, and apply it. `apply` keeps the stash in the list; `pop` drops it only if it applied cleanly.
flags: the full diff of the second stash
turn a stash into a branch when it no longer applies

toolkit.what: Shows what the last merge, pull or rebase actually changed in your branch.
flags: set by reset, merge and rebase to the previous tip
toolkit.when: right after a pull or rebase surprised you

steps.prompt: Match each undo to what it does.
pairs: undo the commit, keep the changes staged
undo the commit, keep the changes unstaged
undo the commit and throw the changes away
add a commit that undoes a pushed commit
bring back an old version of one file

steps.prompt: You meant to drop one commit but ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` on your feature branch. Three unpushed commits are gone from `git log`. What do you run?
options: `git reflog`, find the entry before the reset, then `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`
Nothing can be done: `--hard` deletes the commits
steps.explain: The commits still exist; only the branch pointer moved. The reflog shows where HEAD was, and `HEAD@{1}` is the position just before the reset. The remote does not have them because they were never pushed.

steps.prompt: A merge into `main` (commit `4d1e0aa`) broke production. Ten people have already pulled `main`. How do you undo it?
steps.explain: Shared history is never rewritten: revert adds a new commit everyone can pull. A merge has two parents, so Git needs `-m 1` to know that parent 1 (main before the merge) is the side to keep; without it the revert fails.

steps.prompt: Stash everything, including the new files you have not added yet, with a message.
steps.explain: `-u` includes untracked files; `-a` would also stash ignored files such as `bin/` and `obj/`. `-m` sets the message. `-k` keeps staged changes in place and `-p` asks hunk by hunk.

steps.prompt: Which undo is safe on a branch other people have pulled, and which only on your own unpushed work?
items: `git restore --source=HEAD~2 -- f` then a new commit

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before any reset or rebase, glance at `git log --oneline -5` so you know what you are moving. When something vanishes, reach for `git reflog` first, not a fresh clone. On shared branches use `revert`, never a force-push.
